newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-Vitro looks at life after Anchor.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Vitro looks at life after Anchor.

text.p: Mexican glass-maker Vitro is using the sale of its troubled U.S. unit Anchor Glass Corp to take a fresh look at the rest of its business.

Having completed a final agreement to sell Anchor on Friday to U.S.-based Ball-Foster Container Co for $365 million, Vitro is wasting no time in looking to sell off other assets to reduce its debt further and strengthen its balance sheet.

"We are analyzing our strengths and weaknesses, looking at growth possibilities in each market we are in," Thomas Cantu, Vitro's international director of legal affairs, told Reuters in a recent interview after a letter of intent for the Anchor sale had been signed. "All of our units are being looked at ... the decision about whether we sell X or Y unit will come from that analysis," he said.

Vitro has spent some $90 million on Anchor so far this year -- much more than the $65 million that had been budgeted at the end of last year for a two year period. Anchor accounted for about a third of Vitro's $3 billion in yearly sales.
"We did more to keep Anchor going than probably a lot of other companies would have done," Cantu said.
Vitro decided to sell Anchor after top management decreed earlier this year that all Vitro units had to meet a minimum requirement of 14 percent return on investment.

Vitro will probably take the writeoff on its Anchor investment, estimated at about $400 million, during the third quarter, said Hugo Jaime Garcia, Vitro's director of corporate finance. On the plus side, Vitro will have some $1 billion in liabilities taken off its books, including Anchor's nearly $600 million in secured and unsecured debt.
"Our company will be much more financially healthy," Jaime Garcia said.
Vitro will have some $1.7 billion left on its books, about 80 percent of which is long-term debt.

Jaime Garcia said Vitro wants to continue to reduce its level of debt, probably through disinvestment of assets, and is currently considering raising its proportion of dollar debt to overall debt to lower financing costs.
"We are studying our debt mix. Currently, we have 60 percent peso debt and 40 percent dollar debt. We could raise the proportion of dollar debt," he said.
Company officials say their margin of earnings before interest and taxes versus sales should improve from about 10 percent before the Anchor sale to some 18-19 percent.
Dollar income as a percentage of sales will fall to about 50 percent from 65 percent before the sale, they said.

But officials stressed that dollar revenues are still high enough to give the company a hedge against Mexico's volatile economy and that Vitro still maintains operations in the United States and other countries in Latin America.
Vitro's exports this year will hit about $600-630 million, officials said.
Jaime Garcia said he also sees the company's domestic sales recovering this year as the economy picks up after a deep recession.
"We don't see a very strong recovery, but at least the trend is positive," he said.
"And as things like construction come back on line, things like windows and household appliances should bounce back," Cantu said.
